 Parsons has four children, who are men and women now. They are all spokes of the wheel, and one day his longest son came home angry. The axle shaft of an old secondhand quad wheel he owned had broken six or eight miles from home, and he had to walk that distance, dragging the old wheel after him. He threw it down scornfully and said: "Pa, you can have that wheel. I'm going to buy new." He accepted the gift, to the surprise of his wife, who ridiculed the idea, and thereupon he said that he'd ride it all summer to learn. Three months of hard work accomplished it, and Parsons has ever since been a lover of the bike. Within three weeks he had made trips to villages ten or twelve miles away on several occasions. The following year he secured machine costing 25 pounds, and the past year he has travelled 5000 miles on his wheel, both summer and winter. In every trip, runs to and from his meals he has run over four miles, and on Sundays has run frequently and with great speed 40 or 60 miles, and has covered more in one month than most do in a year. His habits and costume are very simple. He never tries to race, being satisfied with a fair rate of speed. He wears common leather boots, bicycle cap and even a shirt sleeves, carrying a warm sweater and light coat to slip on when dismounting for any length of time. He never rides a wheel in wet weather, and has never known what it is to take cold after a ride. "There are two things I believe in," he said, in an interview as to his habits in riding. "One is that stimulants should not be used by bicyclists who wish to journey without serious results; the other is that the medium position in riding is the easiest and the safest for the cyclist. Throwing myself forward, lightly and still keeping my body level, is the best way of riding. The position does as much for the muscles that people complained of. I believe that position to be the principal"

show you around on the inside. It
might be William Harley, but if he has
gone for piece of tobacco, rap gently
for Charles Sanborn, but provided
Charles is not on the premises, whack
the panel of William Young's door a
few times. Or you could make your
presence known to Patrick Greeley,
sing short refrain under Arthur J.
Johnson's window, or call plaintively
for William Harris. All these families
are camped under one roof—not the
same roof that inspired Evangeline, or
the Psalm of Life, as Longfellow packed
up his valise and moved out of this
house at the age of three months—but
just the same, hospitable roof—

poet first lunched on the life giving
oxygen, Mr. and Mrs. Patrick Greeley
every night dream peaceful dreams.

Greeleys is a colored family, just as
alive to the significance of the dwelling
as any of them. This capacious dwell
ing, with all its wealth of lore, is owned
by John Musgrave, and is kept freshly
painted, not Musgrave, but the dwell
ing, in good repair, as spic and span as
a new house. But the relic hunters

oh, you have to watch them, the rascals,
There are good many visitors there
in the course of a year, and not a few
want to carry away some souvenir.

another tried to get slice of the car-
pet, and still another tried to white a
small slab off the mantel piece. Mrs.

Greeley says they are very obstreperous
at times, while others are orderly and
donate few pennies for the pains.

Longfellow circle right in the block
and having weekly recitals, but owing
to other engagements this phase of
social life will give way the coming
winter to less restrictive functions.

THE REV. J. W. HOOD PREACHES IN THE LAFAYETTE AVENUE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH

The pulpit of the Lafayette Avenue Presbyterian Church at Lafayette-ave. and South Oxford was occupied last night by Bishop J. W. Hood, of the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church. Washington, N. C., Jan. 10.

There was no larger crowd in the courtroom at the opening of the court this morning than at any time since the trial commenced.

It was given out by Brantly's counsel last night that he would not put on any evidence, and everybody was eager to see what turn matters would take this morning.

When Judge Hoke asked if the defendant Brantly offered any evidence, Mr. Simmons, counsel, said, "We offer no evidence at all."

Judge Hoke then asked if the State had further evidence to offer, and counsel answered that they had. A number of character witnesses were offered by the State before to prove the character of other of their witnesses, and all the State's witnesses concerning which questions were asked proved good characters.

On these questions of character the defense in reorganization asked almost every witness for the character of the Bell boys, and Sheriff Bell's character was not questioned at all, but several testified that for some time past Uriah had been wild.

In the rebuttal evidence the State put on two strong witnesses. The Bell boys testified that they did not visit Brantly, and one reputable witness testified that he had seen them both in Brantly's sitting around the fire smoking. Another witness testified that he saw Uriah Bell with a pistol on the Friday before the murder on Saturday night, which was a rebuttal of Uriah's testimony.

Counsel for the State asked him while on examination if he bought a pistol that day, and he said not.

Practically the evidence is all in now. After a few short examinations in a row the arguments will begin. It now looks like argument will commence to-morrow afternoon. A verdict will hardly be had before Wednesday of next week.

Yesterday morning there was a small crowd at the opening of the court, the people being hindered by the rain, but as it was known that Sherrell Bell would be put on the stand a large crowd was soon packed in the room to hear his statements. At this stage of the trial Brantly's wife shows more fatigue than any one interested in the trial.

Brantly seemed a little indifferent as he looked across at the Jury and chewed gum. Uriah Bell looked fresh, doubtless having rested better after having been examined and having that strain removed.

Sherrell Bell looked nervous still, but was neatly dressed in a new suit of clothes.

When Judge Hoke said "Call the next witness," Mr. Beckwith, of counsel for defense, offered an almanac to show the time of twilight at Charleston and Washington on a certain day, which had been mentioned in the trial.

The witness called was Deputy Sheriff Redditt. He lives six miles from Aurora and was the officer that arrested the Bell boys.

"Did you see them and whether anyone else was with them?"

"I asked Ben Thompson to assist me in arresting them. He hesitated, but at last went with me. We found them behind Bonner's store, but saw no one else with or near them."

"Did you see Dave Watson?"

"No."

"If he had been there could you have seen him?"

"I think so."

I read the warrant to them and Uriah Bell looked up and said, "My God, you do not believe it?"

I think Thompson and both said they did not know what to believe.

"Did you have Creole in charge any time?"

"He was there all the time."

"Did he make any statement about Uriah Bell?"

"He had made one to Flowers."

Witness said that Creole stated that he (Creole), Sherrell Bell and Brantly were in the fence corner waiting for Mr. Bonner, and that Brantly had knocked Bonner down and then ran up and helped Brantly throw him over the fence.

He said Creole first stated to him that Brantly shot Bonner twice, but at once corrected it and said only once, and said Brantly ran off and left both the Bell boys with Bonner.

Rodman conducted the cross examination. He asked, "Did Brantly want to see anyone Monday night?" He said he wanted to see Uriah Bell. "Did he want to see anyone Tuesday morning, after his arrest?"

"Yes; he wanted to see several a number."

"Did Creole tell you that Brantly shot Bonner more than once?"

"He made two statements. First he said Brantly shot twice, but he immediately corrected it and said he shot only once."

"When the Bell boys were arrested, did Uriah Bell say he was prepared for the shock?"

"He did."

Witness said that he and Lee Thompson had been working in unison until the Bell boys were arrested.

"What did you tell Charlie Dixon?"

"I told him that Creole had confessed to me and the Bell boys were implicated."

"Did you make any promise to Creole?"

"No."

Mr. Simmons asked if Brantly did not want to see others besides Uriah Bell, and witness said he did.

MOSCOW, May 30.—A terrible panic,
resulting from the great crush of people
at the popular feast here to-day in
honor of the coronation services caused
the trampling to death of many people.


In anticipation of the grand holiday
and popular banquet on the Hodynsky
plains tens of thousands of people began
trooping towards the Petrovski
palace, in front of which the plain is
situated, during the earliest hours this
morning.


By dawn to-day the mass of peasants
about the tables was really enormous,
and they were all desperately hungry,
some of them having tasted by choice
or necessity for nearly twenty-four
hours. The police did everything possible
to keep back the crowd, but sud-
denly the masses, controlled by some
inexplicable impulse, or impatient to
get at the food, pressed forward, swept
everything before them and overturned
tables and benches as if made of grass,
trampling thousands under foot and
crushing the life out of great number
of people. The old and weak naturally
succumbed most.


Owing to the extent of the disaster
and the fact that the plain was sur-
rounded with troops, rendering ap-
proach to the scene of the disaster im-
possible for any body except a Russian
official or physician, long time elapsed
before the full extent of the disaster
became known. The first reports had
said that only few hundred people had
been killed or wounded, but as time
wore on and the ambulances of the
army were kept busy transporting the
wounded to the hospitals of the city and
to the temporary hospitals formed
within the military lines, it began to
dawn upon the people that the extent
of the disaster was very much greater
than at first supposed.


As the day wore on, the Russian off-
icals admitted that the victims num-
bered several hundred. This evening a
bulletin was issued saying that the gov-
ernment officers regretted to be com-
pelled to announce that the victims of
the disaster numbered about 1000, but
by 9 o'clock to-night the news from
the scene of the disaster was that 2,500
bodies had been recovered.


The disaster, it is now explained, was
due mainly to the absence of police,
who had not arrived at go early an hour
in the morning at the scene where the
festivities were to take place. Fully
200,000 persons, of all grades of society,
had gathered together on the Hodyn-
skaje plain at the time the disaster oc-
curred.

COLUMBUS, O., June 24.—The Democratic slate convention adjourned to-night, after being in continuous session all day; it was primarily for convention, and secondarily the budding of a boom for John H. Mclean for the Presidential nomination at Chicago. Of the 678 delegates, 612 voted for free silver and 66 for Morgan. Three men were mentioned by the delegates as being in the running for the Chicago nomination—Mclean, Campbell and Bookwalter. Ex-Gov. Campbell had been favored until the silver tidal wave struck the State, but he was considered too conservative on the silver question. When Ex-Gov. Campbell and his friends arrived here, and found the sentiment drifting for Mclean or Bookwalter, they supported the former, no longer being a silver man, thus ending the Bookwalter boom for President and leaving the field, so far as they are concerned, to Mclean, with the unit being equal. There were two opposing movements, one to instruct for Campbell and one to instruct for Bookwalter. We are informed on good authority the report says, that during the cold weather last winter the engineer found it sometimes impossible to generate more than five pounds of steam for heating purposes, and the proposition to increase the output of the present boilers to eighty pounds pressure to furnish steam for two engines of seventy horsepower each, in addition to that required for heating purposes, is out of the question.

The Executive Committee of the American Federation of Labor, meets in Palmer Building to discuss the introduction of the formulary and the needed supplies for the "Federation" operation, that this introduction and the implementation of the constitutional regulation shall in a public session be presented and explained. This is to be performed, so that the employment of the workers of the underlying organization can be improved. Due to the increasing number of workers, the continuous expansion of the labor-intensive industries. Through difficult conditions, especially the promises of the State-government, one cannot help but feel; the workers' organizations and parties should be helped through a general voluntary labor organization. A general introduction of the constitutional labor law is the right step for the practical solution of the problem of the workers' organization. All other methods and theories must be subordinated to this great cause. The leaders of the "Federation" have instructed their respective branch heads to organize for a wider expansion of the "Labor Union," to verify the Observation-Disclosures and to prepare the necessary points for the suitable time, which Northumberland has prepared. By their order, the members of the "Federation" are to be integrated into the labor organization in groups for the operation and active assistance in the achievement of the common goal; the workers themselves are to be asked in their own way about the constitutional value, about the size of the undertaken work, and about the progress, which they are making, fully informed. The organizers of the "Labor Union" and the leaders of the "Carpenters' International Union" have already begun the constitutional regulation from several hours and their efforts will be supported by the American Federation of Labor's cooperative operation. With vigorous use, it is already proven that both organizations are well coordinated and able, without further difficulty, to carry out their undertaking in the State. With great welcome, one also welcomes the members of the "Carpenters' International Union" who have joined, into whose societies the constitutional law is to be introduced. The regulation is in progress and all branches are working towards it, so that it can be universally accepted.

It seems that something like 4,000 bushels of grain had been put into vacant storage compartment, against which was a lot of coal. This latter caught fire, so it was stated, by accident, and the flames were extinguished with the assistance of harbor tug.

The heat from the burning coal, however, had in the meantime been communicated to the corn, which ignited and is still slowly burning. Seven or eight hundred bushels have already been destroyed and the fire will not be extinguished until the remainder has been removed. It could be put out more quickly, but it is unnecessary, as there is no danger to the vessel, and of course the captain is anxious to save as much of the grain as possible.

been called to join the bivouac of the
dead. "But few meeting years at best,

vember, 1868, he married Miss Susie S.
Reed, who, with one son, survives him.

A large meeting of representatives of the Mesabi iron ore interests on the Negaunee, Vermillion, Gogebic, Menominee and Marquette ranges in the Lake Superior mining region, held at Cleveland on January 20, an agreement was made by which the owners of the various properties are to act together in the prices of ores in order &c maintain rates it will be found necessary to limit production, and accordingly an understanding was reached whereby the output of different mines will be equitably determined. It was stated that the deal was brought about chiefly through the efforts of John D. Rockefeller, of the Standard Oil trust, who has recently purchased extensive iron ore properties in the Lake Superior district.

The promoters of this new trust control practically all the Mesabi ore mines, they will probably be able to carry out their plans for this season's output. The result will be that the iron and steel makers of Chicago, Cleveland, and other manufacturing centers, which depend on Lake Superior ores, will be forced to pay higher prices for their raw material. This will increase the cost of iron and steel in all the forms in which they are consumed, and will injuriously affect hundreds of industries which are engaged in converting the products of furnaces and rolling mills into various forms of manufactured goods. Higher prices will mean that the farmers' nails, fence wire, cotton ties, axes, bolts, and hinges, and all kinds of hardware in general use, will cost more than they do now. In this way the long arm of the ore trust will reach out over the whole country, and its nimble fingers will reach from the people's pockets to rob them of their hard-earned wealth.

The only hindrance to the organization of a national ore trust, which would control all the iron mines of the country and put up prices far above what the Lake Superior ore producers will be able to charge, is the competition of the iron ores of Cuba and Canada which under the reduced duties of the Wilson tariff would come in in large quantities were an attempt made to corner the market. That the duty on foreign ore was not altogether abolished, as provided in the tariff bill when it was passed by the House, distinctively to the advantage of the men who are now trying to make monopoly of the few monopolies who own the principal ore deposits, shows how important it was that their competition should be prevented by high tariff taxes. The duty of 80 cents per ton imposed by protectionist senators means that the ore baron can charge just that much more for their product.

With the threat of higher prices on ore and reduced production, which will mean less employment for labor, it would seem that the time for public favors to the great and powerful iron mining interests was past. It cannot be said that the business is obviously in need of protection. Iron has been mined in this country for about 50 years, and the infant must have six wisdom teeth cut by this time. The Republican House has passed a bill which increases the protection on iron ore, and if the McKinleyites could have their way there, no doubt they would restore the duty of 80 cents per ton, or even impose a higher tax. This is the answer of the Republican party to the people's protection against trust oppression, aided by tariffs which shut out foreign competition. This will give the mine owners more protection, so that they can charge higher prices. Just as soon as we get a chance to legislate in the people's interest, we will find the people like that sort of favoritism. The people's business is to work and pay taxes, not to ask foolish questions about the origin of Republican campaign funds, or why trusts pay in millions to control Congress.

night at the Chutes where they gathered
thousands strong to welcome those candi-
dates of their political faith who could ab-
sent themselves from other engagements
long enough to drop in and be presented
to the assemblage.


B. J. Solomon, president of the West
End Republican Club, introduced District
Attorney W. S. Barnes as chairman of the
evening, and the latter declared in his
opening remarks that he would insist
upon five-minute limit being observed
by each speaker.


Charles L. Taylor, candidate for Mayor,
had few words only to say. He was glad
to see such an aggregation of ladies in the
audience and he prophesied that it would
not be long before woman suffrage would
exist in this State.


"As I believe," said he, "if suffrage being
accorded equally, irrespective of color,
creed, class or sex."


Mr. TAYLOR reviewed his forty years in
the ranks of Republicanism, beginning at
the time he presided at the meeting that
ratified the nomination of Abraham Lin-
coln for the Presidency of the United
States.


He stated briefly that if he were elected
Mayor of this city he would use every ef-
fort to reduce taxes and see that the af-
fairs of the City be administered on the
same principles upon which he conducted
his own personal affairs.


The speaker was strong in his assertion
that in importance the National Issues far
exceeded the local ones, and that the ter-
rible failure made by the Democratic party
in the past four years shows how radical
change is needed.


Without protection it is almost useless to
till the soil of California.


Police Judge Charles A. Low was next
introduced. He is a candidate for re-
election, and the mere mention of his
name by Chairman Barnes brought forth
enthusiastic cheers. The Judge, as did
Carroll Cook and Judge Campbell when
they were presented, said it was not in-
cumbent upon a candidate for the
judiciary to make political speech.


Judge Low stated he desired to have the
people within his hearing friendly and
just. He has done all in his power and
within his ability while on the bench to
care for their interests, and he proposes to
continue doing so should he continue in
office.


Chairman Barnes introduced George W.
Elder, the nominee for Superintendent of
Streets.


Mr. Elder modestly bowed and retired.
But Martin Stevens, the attorney, recited
what he knew personally of the work done
by Elder as the expert for the Street Com-
mittee of the Board of Supervisors during
the past twenty-four months.


He pointed out that in that time Elder
had saved $100,000 for the City and
managed to secure from the Grand Jury
seventeen indictments against the present
Democratic Superintendent of Streets.


The names of Judges John Hunt and
Joachimsthal were mentioned and cheered
to the echo.


In turn the following well-known peo-
ple paid their respects to the crowd: Will-
iam Deane, Edward Wolff, Anna Shaw,
J. R. Aiken and Judge Bonestell.


The Plumed Knights Drill Corps, the
Thirtieth District Drill Corps, the Phoenix
Drill Corps and the Bear Cub visited the
chutes during the meeting.

INTERESTING AND SIGNIFICANT FIGURES COMPILED BY THE AGRICULTURAL DEPARTMENT.

Washington Oct. 25.—The section of foreign markets of the Department of Agriculture will issue tomorrow its circular, No. 10, on the course of wheat production and expectation in the United States, Canada, Argentina, Uruguay, Russia and British India from 1850 to 1895. It shows the average annual product of wheat by quinquennial periods and the very decided increase in the wheat production of the United States, Canada, Argentina and Russia during the last fifteen years; a similar growth would also be shown for Uruguay were the statistics available for the entire period. India alone of the six countries has suffered decline.

The average yearly export of wheat and wheat flour from the United States increased 40 cent from 1850 to 1895; Russia made nearly equal gain; Canada, although rather unimportant when compared with the United States and Russia, shows growth which is proportionately even more.

manner made deep impression upon
the conference and his kind invitation to
Bishop Bowman and the attending ministers, to visit the U. B. conference at
Philomath was greeted with enthusiasm.
W. I. Thompson was reported to have
severed his connection with our church
and his credentials were accordingly revoked.

pastor at Monmouth, was appointed editor and publisher of the Con-
ference Journal and ordered to publish
six copies. The conference treasurer
was also instructed to pay Rev. Fisher
the sum of 50 for his assiduous labor
in revising the journal and thereby
doubling its capacity.


The advertising rates in the Journal
were reduced to $1.25 per card. The
successful solicitors for advertisements
for the Conference Journal were released
from the payment of their allotted Jour-
nals, while the less fortunate were in-
structed to pay $1.00 for two doz. Jour-
nals, their legitimate share.


The resignation of Rev. H. Schuck-
necks as conference treasurer painfully
reminded us of his departure to superin-
tend; we regret to see him leave our conference but bid him
Godspeed.


The committee on worship reported
that T. T. Vincent, from Portland, will
preach this evening at 8 o'clock sharp.
A cordial invitation is extended to all.


The forenoon session of the third day
opened with devotional exercises by
Bishop Bowman who read part of the
2nd chapter of 2nd Timothy, after which,
he earnestly prayed. Then the confer-
ence united in singing the expressive
hymn "How Firm a Foundation."


The minutes of the two previous sessions were read and approved.


The committee on quarterly conference reports reported and the report was
adopted.


The submitted report of the committee
on Sabbath and Tenn. preachers was adopted.

follows: Rev. J. Shupp, Spokane, Wash.,
will preach at the U. B. church; Rev. J.
H. Fisher, Salem, South: Rev. H. G.
Bieter, Portland, United Presbyterian;
Rev. J. Bieter, Salem, Christian church;
Rev. T. T. Vincent, Portland, Baptist
church; Rev. J. Manslarcs, Portland,
Cumberland Presbyterian.


Bishop Thos. Bowman will preach the
ordination sermon in the Evangelical
church. This is one of the most impor-
tant services and the public is earnestly
invited to attend this service at 8
o'clock; at 8:30 p. m. he will ordain
J. Banner and J. D. Rannhart as de-
acons and L. D. Sreyieilcr as elder.


A general mass meeting will be held in
the U. B. church at 7:30 p. m. All
churches will participate, and Bishop
Thos. Bowman will dispense the word of
truth in his usual pungent and forcible
manner.

The statistics of crime IN the United
States. just published in the Chicago
Tribune, are not very encouraging.
The table of figures covers period of
ten years, and the record shows that
while the number of homicides record
ed in 1886 was 1449, there was steady
yearly increase up to 1895, and that
years record shows the number of
homicides at 10,500, or 700 more than
the number in 1894


OF course it must be borne in mind
that during that decade there was
continuous increase of population.
But the growth of the homicide list is
out Of all proportion to the increase of
people. The record is an appalling one
and is calculated to raise the question,
What ia this nation coming to?


Is it going to distance in crime the
densely populated and less civilized
nations of the old world? Such sta
tistics as the above quoted seem to
point that way. AS for the cause or
causes of this homicidal increase,
which amounts to saturnalia of
bloodshedding, there are, of course,
many and widely differing opinions.
Doubtless each of the 1000 ministers
in the United States believe crime to
be largely the result of on-observance
of religious rites and ceremonies,
coupled with growing inclination
among the masses to discard theolog-
ical mysteries and do their own think
ing independent of churchly restric-
tions. Other persons may be in
clined to ascribe the cause of
so much crime to political
corruption, commercial entanglements,
laxity of laws and a still more lax ad-
ministration of them, a growing greed
for wealth. or to any one of several
other possible causes. There is one
class of philosophers, however, who
insist that the most prolific source of
crime is poverty and the fear thereof.


There is certainly considerable plaus-
ibility in this theory. Poverty is
breeder of discord, strife, envy, jeal-
ously and hate. And surely those NOR
bid conditions always tend toward
crime. The more poverty the more
crime, especially where the wealth of
the country is largely concentrated in
the hands of few, and those few are
unmindful of the rights of the
masses. Our social system is bad,
and we'll calculated to widen the gulf
between the very rich and the abject
poor. The abolition of involuntary
poverty would no doubt greatly reduce
the annual criminal record. But no
leveling down process, such as is pro-
posed by modern Socialism, would
cure the evil complained of, even if
such scheme were practicable, which
it is not.


True wisdom and justice point out
a better plan for minimizing the Grim
inal calendar.

ST. LOUIS, June 18.—The silver delegates played a star engagement today. It was brief, but dramatic in the extreme, and easily divided the public attention with the presidential nomination. The proceedings in the convention were of an impressive nature, and all thinking men present felt the gravity of the situation. There were only twenty-three of the silver men who left the hall, but there was a feeling that the hearts of a hundred and more who voted with the majority followed the departing delegates down the aisles they strode along. Nevertheless, the band played on, the convention joined in singing THE Red, White and Blue and the business of the great gathering proceeded as if no unusual event had occurred. The men who walked out held a miniature convention of their own and agreed to spring Senator Teller of Colorado, who has been their leader in the independent movement, as a candidate for president. This plan will be at a meeting to be held tomorrow, when an address will be issued over the signatures of the disaffected delegates who turned their backs upon the convention, and probably by some others. A canvass for signatures was made tonight among the silver men, and the canvassers expressed satisfaction at the success which they met. They are endeavoring to secure the names of all the delegates who voted against the gold plank, but they say they have received words of encouragement from a majority of them. This address will simply suggest Senator Teller's availability as a presidential candidate, upon whom the entire silver vote can be concentrated, and calling upon the voters of all parties who believe in bimetallism to support him.

Although the determination of the ultra silver delegates to bolt was well understood by every man, delegate or spectator, in the great convention hall, few anticipated the scene of tremendous excitement which attended their leave-taking.

The departing delegates had during the night prepared an address to the public in which they sought to justify the step they proposed to take this afternoon. Nothing unusual occurred to mar the perfect harmony which existed on the surface of the convention until Senator-elect FORAKER of Ohio, chairman of the committee on resolutions, presented the platform. After its reading had been concluded Senator Teller presented a minority report and spoke with impassioned eloquence for fifteen minutes in favor of its adoption.

At the conclusion of his remarks the convention by an overwhelming vote laid Teller's silver substitute on the table.

PARTING MANIFESTO.

Senator Teller then sent to the platform and had this manifesto prepared by himself and his colleagues last night. It was as follows:

In announcing the purpose asserted in this paper, it is due to our constituents and to ourselves that there shall be a public showing of indicating facts.

The sole authorized expression of national republican faith from June 3, 1892, until the present date has been the platform adopted in the national convention at Minneapolis. Neither the utterance of state conventions can change the tenor of that platform or abate the sanctity of its binding force. Every delegate to this convention was elected as its adherent and its advocate. True, one of its most important paragraphs has been subjected to such a divergence of action as to make its language unsatisfactory through the intervening time and dangerous if continued in the future, but of the intention there has never been a doubt. It is the rightful province of this convention to revise the party tenets and to do so in this capacity. In the exercise of such authority, has this day made a renunciation of republican law and gospel. With much of the platform we agree, believing that in many essential particulars it compasses the needs of humanity; it affirms the maintenance of right and it declares one elemental principle not only in direct contravention of the expression of party faith in 1892, but in radical opposition to our solemn conviction.

We recognize that in all matters of mere method it is prudent to yield to the will of the majority, lest we should have chaos in parties and in government. But as no announcement by majorities can change existing knowledge or belief sincerely held, so it cannot oblige minorities to abandon or disavow their principles. As sure as it is requisite for peace and progress that minorities shall yield to majorities in matters of mere method, just so surely it is necessary minorities shall not yield in matters of fundamental truth.

ACCEPTED MINNEAPOLIS PLANK

The republican platform of 1892 affirmed that the American people, from tradition and interest, favored bimetallism and demanded the use of both gold and silver as a declaration in behalf of the principle upon which rests the interest of every citizen and the safety of the United States. In factory to the believers in bimetallism, local construction and evasion has it since been demonstrated to be insufficient.

As the declaration of 1892 has been by a single gold standard for our monetary basis and the recent trend of the official power of the party has been in that direction, we can but assume that the gold plank of the new platform, being much more favorable to perpetuate gold monometallism, will be determinedly used in behalf of that idea.

The republican party has won its power and renown by pursuing its purposes courageously and relentlessly; it is therefore only in accordance with the party's history to authorize in the United States to crystallize into law and administration under gold standard in our finances. This, long continued, will mean the absolute ruin of the country and finally of the people.

The American people not only favor bimetallism from the wise instinct which has always been manifest in the affairs of a people destined for the world's leadership. Under the operation of our great demand for advancement we have become to other nations, the greatest debtor nation of the world. We pay vast charges which every year accumulate against us in the clearing houses of the world with the money of the world procured by the disposal of our commodities in the markets of the world. We are a nation of producers, our creditors are nations of consumers. Any system of international or national finance which elevates the price of human product makes that day when it shall be entirely lifted and our country freed financially, as it is politically, from the domination of monarchy and foreign autocracy. Any system!

Be it enacted by the National Council, That from and after passage OF this act, all national certificates shall be issued in the manner hereinafter prescribed, and none other:

First—For all jury or witness fees the clerk shall prepare a roll in triplicate, which roll shall show the name of payee, kind of service, amount paid per diem, number OF days and total amount, and bear the signature duly attested.

Second—For guard and board bill tickets, similar rolls shall be prepared, with an additional record on oath by the sheriff, attesting the correctness OF the roll; and on the first OF every month the clerk shall send one copy of the record to the treasurer and one to the principal chief, and any failure of any clerk to so report, shall subject him to summary suspension from office.

And seem to see more pathos in poor human lives each day.
I am sorry for the strong, brave men who shield the weak from harm,
But who, in their own troubled hours, find no protecting arm.
I am sorry for the victors who have reached success to stand
As targets for the arrows shot by envious failure's hand.
I am sorry for the generous hearts who freely shared their wine,
But drink alone the gall of tears in fortunes drear decline.
I am sorry for the souls who build their own frames funeral pyre,
Derided by the scornful throng, like ice o'er burning fire.

I am sorry for the conquering ones who know not sin's defeat,
But daily tread down fierce desire with scorched and bleeding feet.
I am sorry for the anguished hearts that break with passion's strains,
But am sorrier for the poor, starved souls that never knew love's palms,
Who hunger on through barren years not tasting joys they crave,
For sadder far is such lot than weeping o'er the grave.

I am sorry for the souls that come unwelcome into birth;
I am sorry for the unloved old who wander up the earth;
I am sorry for the suffering poor in life's maelstrom hurled;
In truth, I am sorry for them all who make this aching world.
But underneath whatever seems sad and ill not understood
Know there lies hid from our sight mighty germ of good.
And this belief stands firm by me, my sermon motto, text,
The sorriest things in this life will seem grandest in the next.

Ella Wheeler Wilcox

The Painter.
Nature hath taken her delicate brush,
Her palette and paints and all;
She hath worked in the silence of starlight hush;
She hath worked in the storms loud brawl.
She works, and, lo,
The frescoes grow
On the sides of her ample hall.
She hath tinted the apple with flushes of rose,
She hath covered the pear with white,
And the osier blooms where the honey bees
She hath crowned with golden light.

The leafy sloe
Is draped in snow,
And the celandine stars clean bright.
She hath sprinkled the meadows with olive and gold,
And the cuckoo flowers delicate hue.
She hath kindled the gorse on the wind haunted void
And hath garnished the woodlands anew.
The speedwell's eye,
Pure and shy,
She hath touched with heaven-born blue.
And in and about and around them all
She hath filled in background of green.
The leaf buds burst at her noiseless call
And spread out verdurous screen.
And wearied eyes
In quiet wise
Find rest in the soothing scene.

I. Bruce Dilkes.

Some of the best teams in the city were out, and the brushes were exciting and were watched by throngs of people that lined the sidewalks from one end of the course to the other. Many private equipages, and many wealthy residents enjoyed the sport, and could not resist the temptation to speed. For brilliancy, size and swiftness the crowd that enjoyed the sleighing stands unexcelled, the palmy days on Whalley avenue being eclipsed by far.

Every care was taken to avoid accident. Mounted Patrolman Schroeder was constantly on the course. A new order of things was given from the start. The sleighers were asked to speed from Humphrey street out, instead of from the rock in. This met with general approval, and there was not, in fact, person that failed to fall in with this idea. The course was kept clear of tired horses so that every driver that wished had ample opportunity of showing how fast his animal could travel.

Nicholas Hubinger, with a handsome grey mare, was one of the first on the scene, followed by J. E. Hubinger's family behind the family pair. A Woman In a Wisconsin Prison Declares

That She Murdered the Buffalo Lawyer.

WAUPUN, Wis., April 27.--Minnie Allen, convict 30 years old, serving two years for burglary, has confessed that on the night of April 26, 1894, at Buffalo, she shot and killed Montgomery Gibbs, a lawyer. She lived at Niagara Falls on the Canadian side and claims that Gibbs had promised to marry her. She says she met him on the corner of Bryant street and Delaware avenue and repeated her request that he marry her. He refused, and she shot him three times. She says she makes the confession to clear Clarence Robinson and wife, who are serving life sentences for the murder. She says that at the expiration of her sentence she will go to Buffalo and plead guilty to the charge of murder. She will be released in a few weeks. About a month ago she sent for Mr. Bancroft and told him that she had a secret which had been troubling her conscience for a long time. She then told him she had shot Mr. Gibbs in Buffalo.

She said that she had first met Gibbs in Canada several years before the murder and fell in love with him. He apparently returned her affections, but subsequently deserted her. Becoming desperate at the wrong done her by Gibbs, she threatened his life. But the attorney paid no attention to her, and she says that after he left her in Canada she followed him to Buffalo. Again she pleaded with him and asked him to keep his promise but he refused to do so. She then secured a revolver and on the night of April 26, 1894, followed him as he was returning to his home. At Bryant street and Delaware avenue she met him and repeated the request that he marry her. When he again refused, she shot him down and fled from the city.

With feelings akin to awe, take the

doings of Wamic.


We have enjoyed a fine chinook, in
consequence of which the ground is bare
of snow, and the streams very high.
On the evening of the 9Th very

roads and high waters. For lack of
space we forbear mentioning names, as
there were forty-seven guests present.

conveying forty maidens with a pres
ent to the czarina of a chiseled silver
vase enriched with jewels, and a mag
nificent bouquet.

dation stone and lowered it into place
while the tsar and czarina and the
president resumed their places on the
tribune. M. Boucher read the minutes
of the function which the tsar signed
first, the czarina next and finally Presi-
dent Faure. While the forty maidens
were landing from their boats, the En-
fants De Lutèce chanted "France,
France!"

the czarina, and presented their gifts.
Her majesty accepted them and ex-
pressed her admiration of the presents
at the same time thanking the maidens
with the peculiar grace which has al
ready won the hearts of all Parisians.
The procession was reformed at 4
o'clock, amid the mingled strains of
the Russian anthem and the "Marsel-
laise" and the cheers of the crowds.
The route to the mint was thronged
with wildly cheering people who had
preserved their good nature and pa
tience despite the hours they had
waited for the appearance of the Rus
sian visitors, the procession being at
the time an hour behind the time fixed
by the programme. After their visit
to the academy the tsar and czarina
proceeded to the Hotel de Ville, where
M. Baudin, president of the municipal
council, received them. M. Baudin
read an address expressing the wishes
of the people for the welfare of their
majesties and rendering on behalf of
the city of Paris the homage dictated
by traditions, love of country and faith
in the destinies of the two great friend-

for the good wishes expressed.

including the court of honor, which was
carpeted with fresh flowers and mar
velously decorated (passing on their
way thousands of invited guests,) and
listening to an excellent concert, the
tsar and czarina, at 6 O'Clock, took
their departure for the Russian en-
bassy amid the enthusiastic cheering
of the crowds. Almost all the municipal
officials were present at the recep-
tion. The welcoming of the imperial
visitors could not have been more
hearty if the crowds had been com-

ists.

the decoration of the grand cordon of
St Anne upon the project of the Seine.

This evening, their majesties were en-
tertained at a grand banquet by Presi-
dent Faure and other officials of the
government at the embassy, at the con-
clusion of which they were driven to
the Theatre Francois, where M. Mounet
recited M. Claretie's welcome, after
which Musset's comedy "Caprice" was
performed, followed by a scene from
"The Cid," the performance concluding
with one act of Les Femmes Savann-
tes. The theatre was beautifully dec-
orated with bunting and flowers and a
large and brilliant assemblage was
present.

the tsar and czarina returned to the
Russian embassy.

peach orchards OF the Pacific Northwest
The orchards require irrigation and the water
for this purpose is obtained from small
creeks issuing from the long hillsides, or
is lifted from the river by pumps operated
by current wheels where the current is
sufficient, otherwise by steam engines. The

about July 4, and the crop continues ripen-
ing until the middle of October. The peach

season the apple market has been excellent.

to have put up 100,000 pounds of dried fruit
during the entire season.

St. Paul, Nov. 30.—News from the great
blizzard has been meager today. So far
as learned only five lives have been lost.
Of course nothing has yet been heard
from the remote distances beyond the
reach of the telegraph, and it may be an-
other week before it can be positively
stated that there has not been more seri-
ous loss.

The streets of the snowbound Dakota
towns are being cleared as rapidly as pos-
sible. The extremely cold weather has
frozen the snow until the immense drifts
have reached the proportions of gigantic
icebergs, and dynamite is being used to
blast these out of the way, ordinary picks
and shovels being unable to make any
impression on them.

Stock on the ranges has undoubtedly
suffered heavily, and a fuel famine is
threatened in many of the smaller towns
in the Dakotas. This is by no means a
trivial matter where the mercury is rang-
ing from 10 to 50 degrees below zero.

The railroads are beginning to get their
trains running again. The Great North
ern got its first train into St. Paul from
the snowbound district this morning, and
the Northern Pacific reports that its
line is now open from Portland to St.
Paul. Delayed westbound transcontinental
trains on this road which were being
held at Tower City and Fargo left those
points at o'clock this evening, and the
eastbound trains held at Mandan are
moving and will be due here tomorrow.
The Northern Pacific officials do not an-
ticipate any further trouble and expect to
have trains running on schedule time.

one, dark blue, with tiny white flowers
on it. This was the pride and delight
of his heart, and was worn only on
gala occasions. Val seemed to learn
by intuition how to whisk it into
shape; for small boys seem to have
an instructive feeling for neckties,
just as little girls have for long
dresses.


A tiny girl lifts her short skirts at
a crossing as naturally as a boy
understands the mysteries that, to a
feminine mind, shroud the necktie.


In Val's love for grandpa he could
think of no greater pleasure than to
lend him his treasured tie for a day,
since grandpa actually did not own
one.


"But, my dear, little boy, I don't
know how to tie it," expostulated
grandpa, quite overcome by the
honor; for he knew how dear to the
little boy's heart was his precious
four-in-hand.


"Oh, I'll tie it. It's just as simple,"
said Val, with an air of easy superior
ity. "Well," he added politely, lest
grandpa should think he was casting
reflections, "you can easily learn how.
See, you bring this long end over this
short one, and cross it round it again;
and then bring the same end through
here and pull it down, and flatten it
out so, and there it is," finished Val,
patting it lovingly into final shape
and stepping back, with much pride.

When the death of the reigning pope
draws near, the cardinal secretary of
state informs the dean Of the sacred col
1ege, who summons his colleagues to the
residence of the dying man. The car
dinal vicar issues orders that prayers be
offered in the Roman churches the car

pepe's chapel administers extreme unc-
ton. AS soon as may be after death has
occurred the body must be formally rec
ognized by the cardinal camerlingo,
who, in obedience to an ancient custom,
first knocks thrice on the door of the bed
chamber, Getting no answer, he enters
and taps thrice with silver mallet on
the dead mans forehead and thrice calls
him by naule, No response coming, the
camerlingo declares that the pope is
dead. Thenceforth the camerlingo is the
most important of the cardinals, having
charge of the preparations for the con-
Clave, of the government of the palace
and of the transactions with the repre-
sentatives of foreign powers, to whom
he officially announces the pope's death.
The papal guard of Swiss halberdiers
attends him when he goes out; his arms
are stamped on the medal Of the vacant
see; he takes an inventory of the prop
erty in the palace and affixes seals to the
dead pontiff's papers. But in order to
prevent him from overstepping his au-
thority the sacred college appoints three
cardinals-a bishop a priest and dea-
con-who are called the heads of the
orders, and whose business it is to over
see his acts. They serve for three days.
being replaced by others chosen in rota-
ton.


Meanwhile the great bell Of the capt.
tol, the so called "Paterine, " has tolled
the news to the citizens in Rome. For
merly this was the signal for unlocking
the jails and for unrestrained disorders.
Brokers used to set up booths where
pools, as at horse race, were sold on
the probable next pope, enormous sums
being squandered in this species Of
gambling. More recently that scandal
has been less open. Every one is ON tip
toe with excitement. Churchmen as
well as laymen display an eagerness out
of tune with the grief in which the
church is officially declared to be
plunged.


For during the novendial, or nine
days succeeding the pope's death, the
celebration Of his obsequies and the
mourning for his loss are supposed to
absorb universal attention. His body

in funeral apparel. When masses have
been said over it i'll the presence of the
cardinals, it is removed to ST. Peters,
where, on a magnificent catafalque, it
lies in state, Finally, on the ninth day,
the public funeral-one Of the great
pageants Of the world-takes place, aft
er which the body is coffined and laid
away in the temporary receiving tomb,
to rest there until, when the next pope
dies, it is lowered into the crypt of st.
Peters for permanent burial.


Needless to say, the funeral cere-
monies of the novendial cause no abate-
ment in the preparation for the con-
clave. The day after the pope dies as
many cardinals as happen to be in Rome
meet to confer. The oldest of their num-
Der, the dean of the college, presides
They swear to preserve the utmost Sc
crecy concerning all their proceedings.
They renew their oaths of allegiance to
the holy see, binding themselves to de-
fend and guard the rights, prerogatiyes
and temporal possessions of the church
)up to the effusion Of blood. Then they
discuss questions of immediate urgency,
listen to the reading of the laws govern
ing the election and hear the Gamer
lingo's report Of his business. The con-
gregation reassembles each day, its mem
bers being constantly increased by the
arrival of cardinals from a distance -

LONDON, Aug. 15.—It appears settled that the Czar will leave St. Petersburg August 10th for European tour, and that he will return about November 14th, the program being to visit Vienna, Copenhagen, Paris and Darmstadt.


The French are already working up the excitement. President Faure and his wife will go to Cherbourg and embark on the ironclad Dupuy de Lôme in order to meet the Czar in the channel. The Dupuy de Lôme will be accompanied by the French fleet. On arriving in Paris it has been arranged that the Czar is to alight at the northern railroad station in order to traverse the greater portion of the boulevards on his way to the Russian embassy, where his majesty will stay during his visit to the capital of France.


The French Government offered him the first floor of the Foreign Ministry, which was to be lavishly upholstered, but the Czar declined, preferring to stop at the Russian embassy on the plea that he had to transact the affairs of the Empire on Russian soil.


The Czar's visit to Paris will last a week. The program of the fêtes may not yet been drawn up, but it will include grand banquet, reception at the Elysée Palace, a gala performance at the opera, examinations and big review of troops along the Champs Élysées. It is suggested that the women of France subscribe small sums and present the Czarina with a baby's cot. The idea is certain to catch on.

contest perfect.

People flocked to the ball ground until no
more could be jammed through the gates,
while large crowds of highly excited spectators
lined the adjacent streets for blocks
around. The Alabama team arrived in the
city last night, spending the night at the
Aragon, to be in good trim for the contest
to-day. The crowd that came over from
Alabama brought along a good deal of
money with which to back their team and
the betting commenced early in the day.
At first the odds were on the Auburn team,
which had twice defeated the Georgia boys
and had made a fine record this year in
competition with other towns. Later on,
when the crowd came in from Athens, the
betting took a turn and odds were offered
on the Georgians, who were confident of
victory despite the previous defeats
at the hands of Alabama. The
most of the betting was at even
money. It is a fair estimate to say that
the Athens crowd carried back between
$1,000 and $780, won from the opposition
on the game. At one time the cashier of
the Kimball house had $1,000 in bets in his
safe. The students came with the deter-
mination to back their teams to the last
cent, and many of them were so enthusi-
astic that they put up watches and every-
thing else valuable that they could rem-
der available. The Alabamians were as
game on this line as the Georgians, in
fact, they thought they had soft snap
when they could get even money, and
as a result of this confidence some of them
went home dead broke tonight.

After the game this afternoon the town
was turned into pandemonium. The
Athens boys brought over with them
car-loads of tin horns and cow bells, some
of the horns being of the mammoth va-
riety, capable of making a noise that
might be heard a mile. In the exuber-
ance of their shouts they paralyzed all
sound.

The defeat of the Alabama team to-day
puts honors even between that team and
Georgia eleven has the advantage of one
victory since the formation of the South
ern intercollegiate Athletic Association
under the auspices of which the games
between the southern colleges are now
played. The victory to-day also makes
the Georgians the champions of the
south. Last year the Auburn team de-
feated the Georgians on the field here by
a score of 16 to 6. The year before that
the Georgia team defeated Alabama by a
score of 10 to 6. In another game played
between the two teams Auburn defeated
the Georgians, which now makes the two
stand even in point of victories, each hav-
ing won two games out of total of four
played.

This year both teams had played three
games before they came together for the
battle royal. In these three games with
other colleges, neither Alabama nor Georgia
had sustained a single defeat. The Athens
team had defeated the University of North
Carolina, one of the best teams in the
south, the Suwanee eleven, and the team
of the Wofford college of South Carolina,
while the Alabama team had defeated Mer-
ger, the Georgia school of technology
and the Suwanee team. With this sort of
record, it was apparently to be a battle of
giants to-day. Both teams were as evenly
matched, according to the records made
as could have been desired.

In weight the Alabamians averaged 166
pounds, while the Georgians averaged 185.
Each team had about the same number of
new men, that is five, the balance being
the same who had met each other in pre-

The amount of power expended in playing on a piano has recently been figured out in a way which, if not altogether accurate, is at least interesting. Wagner has not yet been calculated along these lines. —Cassier's Magazine.

Louisville, Ky. Aug. 12—Wheelmen continue to pour into the city from every direction and the metropolis of Kentucky presents the appearance of a city of wheels. The racing at Fountain Ferry track will begin tomorrow, and the sport as a whole promises to eclipse anything seen in the cycle racing line in this country. The men were putting on the finishing touches to-day, and if the weather continues to be fine some sensational contests will be seen. The track is fast and the men are in splendid condition. There was a time when the average wheelman cared little for the sport of cycle racing, but that time is past as is shown by the pouring in of delegations here.

A terrific electric storm last night had the effect of cooling the temperature nicely. The weather to-day was ideal and the streets were fairly thronged with cyclists. A delegation from New York had peculiar sentiment, peculiar because its sentiment was so far from the truth. When wheeling along the streets tonight, they were singing this little ditty in a woeful, doleful tone:

"Oh, dear, how dry are we."

One enterprising manufacturer or rather his assistants, were called down with turn to-day in their effort to work the advertising game to the limit. They received permission to hang their flag, a gigantic affair, on top of the Gait House. They placed the highly colored bunting to the pinnacle of the flagstaff and placed the Stars and Stripes on the same staff, but some distance below. Many remarked the un-American spirit which such spectacle presented, and some of the delegations from the North became so loud in their condemnation that the attention of the Mayor was called to the matter. Mayor Todd came to the hotel and after consultation the offending flag was ordered to be taken down. The Stars and Stripes now waves from the top of the flagpole with nothing above except the sky, and nothing between it and the earth except the hotel.

The bicycle parade this afternoon was a splendid success, and it compared favorably in point of number and general interest with the parades seen recently about New-York. There were fully 200 paraders and at least 5000 people lined the sides along the route of the procession. The manufacturers' display particularly interesting. The parade passed out Third-ave for a distance of several miles over a fine wheeling route such as could be found in any city. The handsome homes along the route were similar to those of Cleveland, or Bellevue-ave, N.Y. The parade ended at Prospect Park, and the entertainment given the cyclists was thoroughly enjoyed.

The watermelon feast was followed by an old-fashioned colored jubilee. There were apple-eating contests between the pickaninnies, buck and hoe dancing and cake walk. Some of the colored damsels performed with grace that would have taken the first prizes at Madison Square Garden. The scramble for the watermelons resembled a football rush, as the melons were tossed to the throng from large wagons on a platform. As soon as the throwing was started the throng rushed forward and crowded in around it, pushing to the platform. It was impossible for the entertainment to proceed without calling for the police. The crowd was so much in the grip of excitement that it was difficult to get the crowd to go back. The suddenness of their movement angered the police, and this seemed to make it on the verge of a riot. The president of the club appealed to the Mayor to adopt different methods. He was told to go ahead and to his best, but the crowd was too large. He went in form and talked to the crowd in earnest, eloquent tones and moved back, arms held out before them as breast shields, or in some confusion the soldiers went.

and stubborn from three different sides,

determined to throw in his guard. With
fine promptness Mortier, with two divi-

alert and ubiquitous, then made his usual
round, and knew when he retired to rest

worth $4,000 of his opponents best men.

Hamilton County Jail, Cell 9.


10 The Public.—Ever since my arrest for complicity in the death of Pearl Bryan, of Greencastle, Ind., great many statements have been made by detectives about the case. Certain newspapers have credited me with which were far more injurious to my case than to the others charged with the same crime. These stories were given to the public in a manner that was bound to carry with them evidence of truthfulness in everything that has been said. I was the scapegoat. Persons here accused me of doing things that I never knew or even heard of. Why this is done I do not know. I am locked up in Jail without funds or friend on earth. I am far away from my home, and the only one I can call friend is my mother, who is too sick to even write me that she knows I am innocent.


On the other hand, my alleged accomplices have everything they can wish for—money and friends. Their welfare is being looked after, while I am left alone to do the best I can. I am not looking for sympathy. All I want is justice. If a jury of Pearl Bryan's peers finds me guilty, I am willing to pay the penalty, but until that time I ask the public to hold back its judgment.


WHAT HE ADMITS


I do not deny the fact that Will Wood sent Pearl Bryan to this city to have an operation performed and that they both knew that she was coming here for that purpose. They also knew that Alonzo Walling was to perform, or had agreed to perform, the operation. She arrived here Monday, Jan. 9. I was at the Union Depot and Walling was at the C. H. & D. depot. We both missed her. The next morning, about 10 o'clock, I received a note by messenger at the college. It asked me to call at Room 1a, Indiana House, and inquire for Mabel Stanley.


I called there at 11:30 and found Pearl Bryan. She said she was here to have the operation performed. She said Will—meaning Woodland—told her to come immediately and everything would be all right. She also said that Will had told her that Walling was ready for the work. I then made arrangements with her to meet Walling that afternoon at Fourth and Race streets. I went to dinner and met Walling, and he made me return to the college, and put it off until night. Later I met Pearl, and we visited numerous stores and places of public interest. I and Pearl went out and met him on the sidewalk and Walling said to her that he had not yet been able to secure suitable apartments for her, and as it was so late he thought it best to wait until the next day, and Walling then left us.


Pearl and I took a ride on the Walnut Hills car, returning downtown about 9 o'clock. We went into Heider's for a little lunch and then I accompanied her to the Indiana House. I then made arrangements to meet her in the streets Wednesday morning at 11 o'clock. I went home. Walling was in bed asleep. He came in late Thursday night, or Friday morning, about 4 o'clock, and took some things off the hook in the closet and put them in Pearl's valise, which he had in the room, and then went out.

I left him there about 8:50 o'clock and went to Albion's on Sixth street and had my hair cut and whiskers shaved off. After that I went to dinner at Heider's and Walling came in. I am still unable to find out any of the particulars as to the whereabouts or condition of Pearl. He told me not to bother myself, as he was taking care of her, and when she was well he would bring her to me.


Walling left me and went to the room. I remained there most of the afternoon, and then went out for a walk until supper time when I went to Heider's. I returned to my room and remained there all night. Walling was there until about 10:30 o'clock, when he went out, taking Pearl's grip with him. I had retired. I saw him no more that night. "This isn't your case, is it?"


He closed his lips, but said not a word.


He replied: "It's all right, keep quiet and say nothing. I've thrown it."

OTTAWA, Ont, Aug 19.-It has been
ascertained on good authority that the
Manitoba school question is as good
as settled and that there will not be
any necessity for remedial legislation.
This decision has been arrived at after
numerous interviews between members
Of the provincial government Of Mani
toba and the Dominion government.
Sifton, Cameron and Watson, Of Mani
toba, have been here for the past few
days and they leave for home perfectly
satisfied that the basis of settlement
will meet the views of all parties. A
caucus of Conservatives today ad-
journed without doing any business,
owing to the small attendance.


Parliament opened this afternoon.
The only business was the election
of J. D. Edgar, of Ontario, speaker Of
the house of commons, and Brodeur,
of Quebec, deputy speaker. The new
opposition made no objection to their
election. The governor-generaFs speech
from the throne will be delivered to-
morrow. The Conservatives held a
PARTY caucus this morning for the cleo
tion of a leader. There is a split in the
ranks over it, and strong opposition
to the choice of Sir Charles Tupper
has developed itself. Sir Charles sug-
gested this morning that the caucus be
postponed until members of the party
who are away fighting in the bye-elec-
tions shall have returned. This was
agreed to and the election of leader
is thus put off The effort to shunt
Tupper is likely to fail.


The session is not expected to last
longer than thirty days. 1t is ascer-
tained upon good authority that the
Manitoba school question has been set
tied on a basis satisfactory to the Man
itoba government, and the new federal
cabinet.


There was large crowd at the open
ing of parliament. Not only was the
crowd of spectators larger than in any
past years, but the attendance of mem
There was no excitement, and every
thing passed off quietly. Premier Laur-
ier, in a short speech, proposed the
Hon. j. D. Edgar as speaker and while
Sir Charles Tupper regretted that a
Frenchman had not been selected, he
made no other objections. Mr.. Edgar
replied, first in English, and afterwards
in French, admidst the cheers of the
French-Canadian members, thanking
the house for the honor conferred on
him.


The speech from the throne tomorrow
Will contain nothing of Importance in
the way of legislation. Reference will
be made to the calling of the session at
this inconvenient season of the year,
the reason being the necessity to pro-
vide for the public service Neither
the public accounts or any of the de-
partment reports for the past year
can be presented to parliament and
reference will also be made to this.
The only measure which will be sub
mitted will be the supply bill A para
graph will be placed in the speech,
stating that an inquiry will be made
during the recess into the tariff with a
view of introducing a measure, which,
while not doing injustice to existing
interests, will materially tighten the
burdens of the people.

DR. B. B. Tyler, of New York, who has
been conducting a series of revival meet-
ings at the First Christian church, closed
his first week last night with a sermon on
"The World's Debt to the Disciples of
Christ" of which the following is
synopsis:

The marvellous success of the Disciples
in gaining adherents is evidence that there
was a place for them and a work. Be-
ginning in the early part of the century,
they now number about 100,000 souls. The
New York Independent last January, in a
statement including all the churches gave
the Disciples more than 10,000. The
rapidity of their growth is un-
paralleled in the history of Christianity.
Not even the great Methodist revival of the
last century equaled in the first fifty or
seventy-five years of its existence the Dis-
ciples of Christ in the rapidity with which
converts were made. What have the
Disciples done and what are they doing to
enlist this interest and move the people
after this fashion?

In the first place, they are teaching
their brethren in all the churches how to
handle the Scriptures in a more rational
and satisfactory manner. They have been
pioneers in the study of the sacred litera-
ture of the Bible in which such in-
quiries as "Who said this?", "To whom did he
say it?", "At what time?", "Under what cir-
cumstances?", "In what connection?", "For
what purpose?" are prominent. The Dis-
ciples were the first to call attention to the
fact that the purpose of the Gospels was
to furnish evidence that Jesus is the Son
of God.

In 1887 or '88, the Methodist Book Con-
cern of New York published a volume in
which the writer called attention to this
purpose of the Gospels. A reviewer spoke
of this feature as original. The thought
he claimed was unique: it belonged to the
writer of that volume alone. The review
was so highly esteemed that it was pub-
lished in the form of a tract and widely
distributed. At that very time, the Dis-
ciples had been for full half century
calling attention to the fact that the Gos-
pels were calculated to produce faith; that
the book of Acts was intended to show be-
lievers how to come to an assurance of
pardon and how to become members of
Christ's holy church; that the general pur-
pose of the Epistles was to show the ap-
plication of Christian principles to the
solution of life's perplexing problems while
the Apocalypse, or book of Revelations,
was intended to show forth, after the
Oriental fashion, the glories of the future
life. The Disciples have from the first
called attention to the fact that the re-
ligion of the Jews is described in the Old
Testament, while the religion of the Chris-
tians is set forth in the New: that the Old
Testament is divided into the Law, the

Testament is divided into the Gospels, the
Acts, the Epistles and the Revelation. The
world owes a debt of gratitude to the
Disciples for their work in this depart-
ment.

The Disciples, to their honor be it said,
discovered in modern times, brought out,
exhibited, explained and showed the place
of the creed of Christianity. They said:
Christianity has its creed without reference
to its denominational divisions. We have
the Greek, the Latin, the Anglican, the
Protestant conceptions of Christianity, and
in Professionalism we have the Lutheran,
the Presbyterian, the Baptist, the Con-
gregational, the Methodist and other con-
ceptions of Christianity but behind all
these and beneath is a statement of the
essential faith to which all with one voice
subscribe. The creed of Christianity is
this: Jesus of Nazareth is the Christ, the
Son of the living God and the Savior of
men. All who profess and call themselves
Christians subscribe to this. It is the only
creed to which the Disciples adhere. They
claim that a heart subscription, not a
merely intellectual, but a heart subscrip-
tion to this creed is so far as faith is con-
sidered sufficient to make one a Christian.

appreciated. To cut loose as did our
fathers from the great historic creeds of a
divine Christianity and anchor themselves
upon a divine creed was an unusual fear in the history of re-
ligion. This creed includes all essential
Christian truth. It answered that purpose
of a creed in the Apostolic church; it
answers that purpose now, and will do
so for all time. The world is in debt to
the Disciples.

In spite of attempts to conceal the
fact, it has leaked out that Rev. Dr. W.
W. Landrum, pastor of the Second Bap-
tist church of this city, was on last
Sunday called to the pastorate of the
First Baptist church of Nashville, Tenn.
The last-named church is the wealth-
iest and most influential of all the Bap-
tist churches in Tennessee. It has a
house of worship which cost $4,000, and
is the central Baptist force of Nash-
ville.

The call was not only enthusiastic, and
unanimous, but the church delegated
Dr. J. N. Frost to come to Richmond and
plead with Dr. Landrum to give a favor-
able response. Dr. Frost reached the
city yesterday morning, requested Dr.
Landrum to meet him at the Jefferson,
and spent good part of the day try-
ing to show the Richmond divine that
his path of duty evidently laid toward
the Tennessee metropolis.

What Dr. Landrum's decision will be
cannot now be told, since it has not been
his purpose to let these facts go into
the public eye to make the Second Baptist church peo-
ple believe that Dr. Landrum would
leave them for any other charge.
WILL BE CONSIDERED.
It is taken for granted that Dr. Lam-
drum will give the matter due conside-
ration and follow his convictions. He
has been pastor of the Second Baptist
church, this city, for over a dozen years,
and is thoroughly identified with Rich-
mond in all of its interests, and his
departure would carry sorrow to thou-
sands of homes. Besides, he is greatly
beloved and honored by the Baptists of
the whole State; and, as far as his own
church is concerned, it would be a unit
ready to strive even unto blood against
his being taken away.

I need not be added that the salary
offered by the Nashville church to Dr.
Landrum is worthy the great church
which called him. It is proposed in this
call to meet every expense necessary for
his removal to and comfortable estab-
lishment in Nashville. It is also said
that the pastor of this church is, by rea-
son of the fact that he is pastor, the
most commanding figure among the many
thousands of Baptists in that State; so
Dr. Landrum should accept he would
at once come to the front in the Bap-
tist forces of that State.

ABILITY AS A LEADER.

Dr. Landrum possesses a high degree
of ability for leadership, and if he sees
it to be his duty to go to Nashville he
will have almost unlimited opportunities
to serve his denomination.

This is not the first call that Dr. Lam-
drum has received since he has been
in Richmond. He was rendered pasto-
rates in Memphis and Louisville, and
calls have been quite
numerous. Not one of these calls, how-
ever, was fully the equal of the Nash-
ville call, and this last distinction shows
the great honor in which this Richmond
divine is held. One of them was re-
ceived a year or so ago, and Dr. Lan-
drum announced his intention to accept,
but that evening the members of his
congregation brought such pressure to
bear upon him that he reconsidered his
determination, and stated to his people
that he expected to spend the rema-
inder of his days among them, and be buried
in Hollywood.

Grace-Street Baptist church will never
come to its flood. Last night, although
all the other churches had their prayer
meetings, the First Presbyterian church

was crowded, not only in its auditorium
and galleries, but in its lecture-room, be-
hind the church, with scores of young

ton preached on "The Way of Salva-

ed to throw a spell over the vast con-
course of people. About twenty per-
sons came forward to make their con-
fessions, and the unconverted all over
the house manifested the greatest signs
of interest and concern. The meetings
will continue.

mond College has become so marked
that it has been determined to suspend
the exercises of the college at noon
to-day and tomorrow for special revival
services. Drs. Hatcher and Broughton
will conduct these meetings, and the pub-
lic will be cordially welcomed.

spoke cheerfully of the building fund for
his new church. He said that he re-
ceived several hundred dollars yester-
day, unsolicited, from his own people,
and that quite a goodly number of gifts
came to his hands from other sources
during the day. Inasmuch as many
persons are receiving these donations
for the new church, he said it would be
impossible to report the names of the
donors at present. Among the contribu-
tions received yesterday were The Lit-
tle-River church, in Loudoun county,
$3.50, of which Rev. C. W. Trainham
(an old Grace-Street member) is pastor;
Rev. O. L. Martin, of Anderson, S. C.,
sent Dr. Hatcher $1.50 to be used in re-
establishing his library; W. S. Forbes
sent a check for $500,
which gave Dr. Hatcher and his people
peculiar satisfaction: In the Doctor's
mail there came a letter from Rev. J.
Calvin Stewart, now at Clifton Springs,
N. Y., with not only an expression of
that minister's sympathy, but with a
check for the building fund. That after-
noon among those who professed con-
fession in the revival was an interesting
youth who reported that it was his
desire to unite with Mr. Steward's church
in this city. Dr. Hatcher mentioned
the incident, that it would be inexpres-
sibly delightful to every one if he could
know that every one who had thus re-
membered his afflicted people might be
richly rewarded in spiritual blessings.
Rev. J. W. Mitchell, of Portsmouth,
has been in the city for several days.
He came to engage Dr. Broughton to as-
sist him in revival services in his
church.

Sunday, and reports received are to the
effect that he made a most favorable im-
pression upon Dr. Broughton's flock.

But the contemplation, if we look a little more closely into the matter, may not continue to be altogether of approximating wonder. There may possibly enter into it elements that may give rise to disturbing reflections. Let us extend our gaze from the contemplation of the increase in wealth of New York City alone in the one year 1895 to a contemplation of the increase in wealth in the three Eastern States of New York, Massachusetts and Pennsylvania during the census decade 1880-'90, and compare with the ten years increase in wealth of those three States the ten years increase in wealth of a large group of less wealthy States of the Union. The figures, we may remark, which we are going to use, are the official figures of the United States Census Bureau, and they are as accurate therefore as anything obtainable. Nobody needs to be scared by the figures; for, in addition to their being wonderfully significant figures, they are the simplest in the world.

The combined population of the States of New York, Pennsylvania and Massachusetts, was 13,494,810; the population of the twenty-five States, Maryland, Delaware, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Tennessee, Kentucky, West Virginia, Ohio, Indiana, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, Missouri, Iowa, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Nebraska, Kansas, Texas, Colorado and Wyoming was 81,432,550. The twenty-five States, that is to say, had nearly three times as many people to help on the accumulation of wealth during the decade as the three Northeastern States.

The twenty-five States had thirteen times as much territory to operate on as had the three States; and they had $81,704,552,186 more of assessed wealth than had New York, Pennsylvania and Massachusetts together at the beginning of the decade 1880-'90 which we have under review.

Well, now, the twenty-five States named evidently had a magnificent start in the race for wealth during 1880-1890 as compared with the three northeastern States, for they had an greater capital, three times as many people and thirteen times as much territory. The territory of the twenty-five States being at least as prolific as that of the three States, and the 100,000,000 people of the twenty-five States being, man for man, as industrious and capable as the 10,000,000 people of the three States. Readers of the Times-Democrat will have no difficulty in coming to the conclusion that the Twenty-Five States with their immensely larger territory, their immensely larger population and their immensely larger capital to start with in 1880, ought in combination to have far the three States in the increased accumulation of wealth in 1890. Our readers will readily agree that, if the twenty-five States with their almost incalculable advantages over the Northeastern trio in 1880, did not show a far larger increase of assessable wealth than the trio, there must have been and must be some forces at work which greatly handicapped the twenty-five States of the South and West and disseminated in favor of the Northeastern three, in the pursuit of wealth.
