WAS poor in promise at opening, there were half fifty persons in the Conference-room. Bishop came in late, having mistaken the time, and the preachers dragged slowly after, depressed by the heavy mist. Later on people frightened themselves a little though the weather did not, and by noon the house was nearly full.

The entire session was consumed in routine work, but the proceedings were not without interest to the members and the spectators who filled the galleries. There were no speeches, but there was an abundance of innocent wit and good feeling prevailed throughout the session.

ENCOURAGING EDUCATIONAL REPORT.

The report of Dr. J. J. Bigham, secretary of the Board of Education, was read. The report shows that $2,000 were raised by the several conferences for the work of the board. The Children's-Day collection amounted to $1,000; and $1,925 was raised for Paine and Lane Institute. The secretary is gratified with the cordial co-operation which he has received from many of the preachers and laymen in getting the work of the Board under way. The colleges are in prosperous condition and are all reported distinctly Christian.

THE SUNDAY-SCHOOL OUTLOOK.

The report of Dr. James Atkins, Sunday-School editor, shows that there has been an increase of 15% in the number of Sunday-school pupils in the Southern Methodist church, making a total of 111,000. Quarterlies have a combined circulation of 652,000, an increase of 5,000. The circulation of the smaller lesson papers has decreased. The observance of Children's Day has been neglected in many sections.

REVIEW OF THE FIELD.

Question "Are all the preachers blameless in their life and official administration?" was recalled, and presiding elders made their reports and passed the usual examination of character. All the reports were encouraging, indicating progress in every department of church work notwithstanding the terrible financial depression from which every district has suffered. Rev. W. E. Eldick reported that one church on the Farmville district paid more for missions than was raised on the whole district paid last year. The amount approximates $500; he paid high tribute to the work of Rev. W. W. Lee, the evangelist, who contributed largely to the success of the revival efforts of the year.

A REMNANT FOR GOD'S ALTAR.

Rev. M. P. Wright spoke eloquently of the noble people on his district, robbed, pillaged and plundered by the hard times, gathered from the wreck of their fortunes remnant for God's altar. He said that "a lady brought two gold dollars which belonged to her dead baby to her steward and asked him to pay the pastor for her, and keep the gold treasures until she could redeem them."

The following ministers, who have been in the Conference two years on trial, passed the examination of character, and were advanced to the class of the third year: W. S. Pace, N. J. S. Colonna, Jr., J. L. Parrish, L. R. Williams, G. R. Gibbs, D. W. Reed, W. T. A. James, T. T. Wingfield, G. W. Jones, R. R. Johnson, T. W. Davis, G. W. Dyer, Roy T. J. Potts, who belongs to this class, being detained at home on account of sickness, was continued on trial.

GETTING AT THE FACTS.

In the examination of the character of the Young men, Bishop Duncan exhibited a remarkable talent for getting at the bottom facts. He not only got at the facts, but he made every one else see them.

The following ministers, who have completed the conference course of study, passed the examination of character, and were elected to elders orders: T. J. Dadmun, R. E. Beadles, L. R. Hill, J. R. Rev. J. Y. Chitty, of this class, having early in the year surrendered his credentials, was dropped from the conference roll.

Dr. H. T. Johnson, of the same class, but already an elder, passed the examination of character.

A presiding elder, speaking on the work of one of these preachers, said, "Bishop, he was born pious."

"That's heresy," said Dr. Peterson.

"For we need not be born again, if he was born pious."

Presiding Elder: "If you please, Bishop, such is the kingdom of heaven."

Bishop Duncan: "Very good, you and Brother Peterson settle that."

Rev. Clark, who was readmitted into conference at the last session, and appointed to Trinity church, Norfolk, but resigned his charge before the close of the year, passed the examination of character.

Revs. T. T. Kesler, S. J. Battin, T. T. Merritt and J. D. Langley were elected to deacon orders as local preachers.

Win Mercer was in the hunt again Saturday. He is a pitcher sure enough. With a high-class team to back him up, both at the bat and in the field, he would come pretty near winning every time he went in the box. As it is, with a tail-end team behind him, he wins four out of every five games. He is the best pitcher in the league, everything considered. The Reds were the only team that have given him very poor reception this season.—Exchange.

No player created more tricks or played faster ball than Kelly, Williamson, Burns, Pfeffer, Flint, Corcoran, "Goldy" and the other boys of the famous White Stocking. I'd bet 800 on the game, always betting on their own team, of course, with outsiders. I'd go to Corcoran and say: "Larry look little doubtful today; guess we're beaten." "How's that?" Larry would ask. "I've just bet you my new hat I'm right," I'd reply carelessly. Corcoran would go in and pitch like a horse and win his new hat, while Kelly got his hundred.

Jack Doyle's return to the game was in the nature of a surprise, welcome it was, unexpected to the Baltimore fans. He got right into the game, too, and played all the week with his old-time vigor. I'm less that ankle begins to trouble him again; at present there being no signs of such thing, he will go right on at first.

Bill White, the famous eye-glassed pitcher, who was never known to hit ball, was at bat one day, and a man in the press room remarked that White would someday make a home run. There was much merriment and one man offered to bet his $50 gold watch against a cent that White would make no homer on this particular occasion. "Good bet, even if I lose," said the other, and watch and cent were duly staked. Hardly was the wager deposited when White hit that ball with a terrific paste and started around the bases. The ball went on and on; so did White, and the man of the gold watch turned deadly pale. Rounding third base, White stumbled and fell, floundered around, regained his feet, went ahead and was caught by a tiny margin at the plate. He who had put up his watch seized his timepiece, letting the cent drop in his excitement, and exclaimed: "Gentlemen, if I get out of this ground alive I shall never see another ball game!"

The Anderson & Hicks Lumber Business Gets Into the Courts.

Valdosta, Sept. 25—The extensive lumber mill business of Anderson & Hicks, at Melrose, has been placed in the hands of a receiver. E. W. Lane of the Merchants Bank of this city, having been appointed receiver.

The causes which lead to the receivership are said to be a disagreement between the partners, or rather desire on the part of one of them to get out of the business. The assets of the firm are about $4,000 and the liabilities are placed at from $4,000 to $4,000. The mill was recently equipped with splendid new machinery, and is one of the largest plants in this section. It is generally understood that the business was almost wholly owned by Mr. W. H. Anderson of Brunswick, and it was at his request that the receiver was appointed.

The mill will be operated for awhile by the receiver and it is said that in this way enough money can be realized to settle nearly all of the debts of the concern. None of the creditors here believe they will have any trouble in getting their money dollar for dollar, though it may be several months before all of the debts are liquidated.

A Royal Arch chapter of Masons was established here Friday and Capt. S. T. Kingsberry was made high priest of the chapter. It is understood that twenty members have been elected to that degree, and that fifteen of the number had the degrees conferred upon them Friday night. Some of the most prominent Masons in the state were here to officiate on the occasion.

Echols superior court convenes to-morrow, and nearly all of the local lawyers will go down from here in the morning. The trip is twenty-five miles through the country, and each session of the court there is vigorous talk of trying to consolidate Echols into this county and Clinch. There will be more business in the court tomorrow than has been in several sessions, there being one murder case and a case against three white men charged with burglarizing a car at Alexanderville four years ago. They are to be prosecuted by their bondsmen, having failed to appear at former terms of the court, and their bonds being forfeited.

Hon. W. G. Brantley is expected to speak at Echols county court house to-morrow, and a large crowd will no doubt be present to hear him.

The long drought here has had the effect of almost drying up all the streams. Dukes bay, which is usually full of water, is as dry as bone, and the river, four miles from here is not three feet wide in many places. There are indications of rain this evening, however.

Speaking of the appointment of a receiver for the property it says that there appears to be no occasion for undue alarm, and that the receivership is designed solely to give the company protection from unfortunate creditors until it can be rehabilitated.

But isn't it remarkable that property having such an immense volume of business should become bankrupt? Its earnings haven't fallen off. On the contrary, they have steadily increased from year to year. That being the case there must have been something radically wrong with its management. Only few years ago the road was in trouble and it was saved through the wise management of Mr. Spencer, now president of the Southern railway. Holden, who had the body disinterred and an autopsy was held the 10th of February, the result of which will appear during the trial.

Last Friday and Saturday an inquest was held at the office of Hon. Frank Plumley, the result of which is yet not made public. But it is said that it was found that Marsh came to his death by poison.

The hearing to see if there is evidence enough to bind Mrs. Marsh and William Buzzell over until the next term of court commenced Monday morning before Justice H. H. Thayer, assisted by Prosec. Chas. Dole, Zed S. Stanton and Frank Plumley for the State, C. D. Edgerton and ex-Gov. Dillingham for the defense.

H. H. Boss was the first witness. He testified that he met Mrs. Marsh one day going for a physician and he asked her husband's condition and she replied she did not think he would live.

The second witness was Hiram Henry, a neighbor of Marsh's. He was at Marsh's house Saturday night before death. Marsh was in bed. Dr. Johnson, William Buzzell, and two Toddlers were at the house. Marsh seemed in great pain in the stomach and bowels. The witness testified he was there the Wednesday before Marsh died. Mrs. Marsh asked him if he was a good hand to lay out corpse. While there Buzzell went to the cupboard, got a teaspoonful of white powder and mixed it in some liquid and gave it to Marsh. The witness testified to appearances at times of trouble between Marsh and his wife.

The next witness was Mrs. Charles Andersen of Brookfield. She testified that Buzzell and Mrs. Marsh were at the witness's house to dance some time since without an invitation. Mrs. Marsh was more intimate with Buzzell than her own husband. She stood on the floor with her arm about his neck.

The fourth witness was Mabel Hill, aunt of the late George Marsh. She testified that Mrs. Marsh was away when Marsh was dying, but later came home with Buzzell.

The next witness was George H. Bailey, who was called to the Marsh house at a. m. on the morning of his death. He had an interview with Mrs. Marsh during which time she sat with her arm around Buzzell's neck in the parlor. The court adjourned.

Unlike yesterday, Mrs. Marsh appeared at ease when the court convened Tuesday morning at 11 o'clock. DR. Daniel Johnson Jr. was the only witness examined. He testified he had been Marsh's attending physician. In his examination of Marsh his only peculiar symptom was that his pulse was only 15. He said he left no unmarked white powders. I asked for a post-mortem examination of Mr. Marsh and continued the witness "but Mrs. Marsh said she did not want him cut up and appeared to feel badly. It was the first time she showed grief. Sunday it occurred to me he had some poison in his system perhaps from the water. I never thought up to Tuesday noon he had any other disease than biliousness. I knew that his distressed condition was caused by white arsenic. I should never be satisfied to think that he died from poisoning alone. I thought he died of heart failure induced by some cause unknown to me. The tablets I administered were slightly green; I left no white powders in powder form.

The first witness of the afternoon of Tuesday was Prof. J. Linsley of Burlington, connected with the medical department of the U. S. N. J. He testified that he was engaged by Capt. John J. Big Indian, N. Y. Aug. 2—Winnisook Lodge
high up in the Catskill Mountains, ten miles from
telegraph station and perfect in isolation as it is
beautiful in situation, sheltered William J. Bryan and
his wife tonight. Mr. and Mrs. Bryan are the
guests of Major James W. Hinkley, chairman of
the Democratic State Committee; Thomas H. Bene-
dict, the Federal Public Printer, Charles A. Schultz
of Rondout, and other members of the club which
maintains the lodge. The Winnisook Club by the
way is not a political organization, and Major
Hinkley, through whom the invitation to Mr. Bryan
was extended, says the visit is intended to be pure-
ly social, and has no connection with Democratic
politics in New York State. It was 5 o'clock this
evening when Mr. and Mrs. Bryan, under escort of
Mr. Schultz and Mr. Preston, ex-Examiner of State
Banks of New York, reached the Lodge after
a long drive over mountain roads from Big Indian.
They had enjoyed the drive immensely, and the
warmth of their reception by the members of the
Winnisook Club, their wives and members of their
families made it all seem like homecoming in-
stead of a greeting in the enemy's country.
Major Hinkley, Mr. Benedict, Mrs. George S.
French, of Washington, Mrs. Schultz and others
received Mr. and Mrs. Bryan as they alighted from
their carriages in front of the Winnisook Lodge
house. The sojourners gathered there gave the
club veil and the candidate and his wife bowed
their thanks. Then Mr. Benedict and his daugh-
ter Mrs. French took them in charge and con-
ducted them to the Benedict cottage, which over-
looks the pretty little lake which forms one of the
chief attractions of Winnisook Lodge. Mr. and
Mrs. Bryan had supper in the clubhouse with their
many hosts, and later in the evening were
entertained there informally.


Summer boarders mingled with hardy handed
farmers greeted Mr. Bryan at Phoenicia. Three or
four only of the score of people at the ham-
let of Anaben came forward to shake hands with Mr.
Bryan. A large number of summer boarders were
at Shandaken. One man who had been imbibing
a little too freely worked the crowd up to the
height of his enthusiasm. When he paused, the
people gave three cheers for Mr. Bryan and three
cheers for his wife.


A large crowd was gathered at Big Indian, and
everybody seemed to be enthusiastic. They pushed
and crowded around Mr. and Mrs. Bryan as they
left the train, and it only by dint of hard work
that the broad-shouldered young candidate could
make a way for his wife and himself. The nominee
was conducted to the porch of the hotel, and here he
made a few remarks. Places all along the ten
miles of rough road from Big Indian to Winnisook
Lodge people were gathered to see the Democratic
candidate. Most of them were summer sojourners
and they had a good time in making as much noise
as possible for the benefit of Mr. Bryan. An old man
butcher noted Catskill guide greeted the candi-
date when his house was reached by means of a
double barreled shotgun salute at Onerega,
a little mountain village, with considerable enthusiasm
shown.


Upper Red Hook, N. Y. Aug. 2—Mr. and Mrs.
Bryan left Upper Red Hook for Winnisook Lodge
in the Catskills, at noon to-day. They drove in
the river to Rondout. They were accompanied to
Rhinecliff by their hosts, Mr. and Mrs. [unintelligible].


Kingston, N. Y., Aug. 2—Reaching Rhinecliff,
Mr. and Mrs. Bryan were met by Charles
A. Schultz, representing the Winnisook club, John
Y. Schoonmaker, superintendent of the Cornell
Steamboat Company, and John G. Van Etter, of
Kingston, a delegate to the Chicago Convention.
At 2 o'clock the party crossed the Hudson to
Kingston Point in a tug and the candidate was
greeted at the landing by several hundred people
who so effectually barred his progress that quite a
struggle ensued before he could reach the Ulster
and Delaware train waiting to take him to Big
Indian. A special car had been attached to the
train and standing on the rear steps of his car,
Mr. Bryan in response to loud calls, made a short
speech. He said:


"I don't care to make any speech, never see people
gathered together without wanting to make speech.
I believe I represent the best interest of the people.
I believe I'm platforms—platforms not to

man has to protect his large interests. But I must
close, for if I talk much longer, I will have made

that that momentous Commission could not pay

throughout the country that the emergency out OF
which that Commission had originated had passed.

had dwindled down to mere matter OF office rent.

heard the closing arguments OF counsel on the
sugar bounty cases, by Joseph J. Choate, in be-
half OF the claimants and by Solicitor-General
Holmes Conrad for the Government. In the course
of his speech Mr. Choate briefly paid his respects to
Controller Bowler, whose action made the litigation
necessary and who auditor OF the argu-
ment throughout. He was speaking of the power
OF Congress TO make the appropriation which had
been withheld from the claimants, contending that
the courts had jurisdiction to review that action;
why, he said, the cases are here merely by ac-

come here to get it removed so that the wheels
might be allowed TO go round.

It is evident that a number of improvements in public roads and buildings, wharfs, etc., are an immediate necessity in order to develop the country properly, and that it is impossible to pay for all this out of the current receipts.

The appropriations asked for under this Loan Act are not to hand as yet, but they will be in the neighborhood of one million dollars, and therefore limit to this amount, as recommended, seems sufficient.

It is desirable that home capital should have the preference if the bonds are taken at par, or even at 2 per cent. discount. If sufficient bonds cannot be sold on the Islands, then there seems to be no reason why they should not be placed in the market in San Francisco, New York and London. It is true that the interest will have to be sent out of the country, but against this the capital has to be invested here first of all, to enable the Government to carry out the intended improvements, which will pay in indirect taxes more than their cost and interest.

Public improvements will beneficially affect all business enterprises, by the circulation of more money, and will especially benefit the laboring classes during the present hard times. The low rate of interest will no doubt be satisfactory to capitalists, but at the same time the Government should not be obliged to wait till large dividends and profits enable our resident capitalists to make investments in Government bonds. Suppose the dividends should be small and the parties not disposed to take up the bonds on Government terms, then all improvements under this Loan Act will have to be stopped and progress delayed. In fact the Government would be placed in an unpleasant position between capital and labor.

It is also impossible to prohibit the sale or transfer of bonds acquired in Honolulu to any parties abroad, in the United States or Europe, and the only difference would be that private parties earn the profits which the Government aims to secure for itself.

Therefore, although favoring Hawaiian investors, no terms can be made, which will be solely beneficial to these parties.

There is no reason to feel against foreign capital, as we have needed it in the past and will need it in the future to build up and strengthen our old and young industries. If these foreign loans should tend to reduce the regular rate of interest on the Islands, there will be no harm done, as a low rate of interest generally produces prosperity, or at least assists enterprising men to make their ventures or undertakings remunerative to all parties interested in the same.

THE financial plan underlying the idea of having these bills, Nos. 20 and 21, separated, although No. 21 is merely an appendix to No. 20, seems plausible and commendable.

Some of the details are certainly debatable, and it cannot be the province of a single member to define the same.

Respectfully submitted,
W. SCHMIDT

The necessary arrangements have been planned for as regards the kit and other appurtenances and all will be in readiness for the first league game at home Nov. 15, with our old time opponents, the Alamedas, representing Bath in the league.
